issues.description: The abstract and throughout the paper the authors claim to use a 'national probability sample' and a 'nationally representative sample', but the Methods section reveals participants were recruited through 'the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington'. This is a convenience sample of undergraduate psychology students, not a national probability or representative sample. This is a fundamental and pervasive misrepresentation of the sample that undermines all generalizability claims and the framing of the entire study.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.

issues.description: The abstract describes 'a national probability sample over five years' and the Discussion states 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' These claims are directly contradicted by the Methods, which describes a university psychology pool sample. The paper also references the NZAVS website for full details, implying the data come from the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (a genuine national probability sample), yet the described sample (N=374, mean age 19, 68% female, recruited from introductory psychology pool) is clearly not the NZAVS. This creates profound confusion about the actual data source.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people's willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years.

issues.description: The sample described (N=374, mean age 19.42, 68% female, recruited from introductory psychology pool) is indistinguishable from a student sample, yet the paper repeatedly contrasts its findings with Stanley et al.'s [14] student sample and attributes differences to sample type (general population vs. students). The entire theoretical framing of the Discussion—that SDO is a stronger predictor in general population samples—rests on this false distinction. The paper's own prior work (Stanley & Wilson [22]) found SDO-environmentalism associations are weaker in student samples, yet this paper uses what appears to be a student sample while claiming general population status.
issues.quote: It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.

issues.description: The Methods section defers critical sample information to an external website ('Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website'). A manuscript should be self-contained. Readers and reviewers cannot evaluate the study without knowing attrition rates, recruitment procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and how the longitudinal sample was constructed. This is especially important given the apparent contradiction between the claimed and actual sample type.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The chi-square statistic is extraordinarily large (χ²(2279) = 36511.73), indicating very poor absolute fit. The authors dismiss this by noting it is 'affected by model complexity' and rely on RMSEA and SRMR. However, a chi-square ratio of approximately 16:1 (df ratio) is far beyond acceptable thresholds even accounting for sample size sensitivity. The CFI of .86 is also below the conventional .90 threshold for acceptable fit and well below the .95 threshold for good fit. Accepting a model with CFI = .86 without substantive justification or model modification is problematic.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The RMSEA confidence interval is reported as [.025, .026], which is an impossibly narrow interval (a range of only .001) and is almost certainly a reporting error. Confidence intervals for RMSEA are typically much wider. This appears to be a copy-paste or formatting error that calls into question the accuracy of all reported statistics.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate use of path analysis without measurement model
issues.description: The authors use path analysis (observed variable) rather than structural equation modeling with a latent variable measurement model, despite using multi-item scales for all three constructs. This means measurement error is not accounted for, which attenuates cross-lagged coefficients and inflates autoregressive paths. Given that the scales are short (6 items each) with modest reliability (e.g., SDO α=.69, RWA α=.70), this is a meaningful concern. The authors do not justify this choice.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: Reliability coefficients are mentioned in passing ('Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case') but only the diagonal of Table 1 appears to show reliability values (.69, .70, .76). No reliability values are reported for Time 2 through Time 5, which is important for evaluating measurement consistency across waves, especially given that one RWA item was missing at Time 2.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures.

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but was included at all other time points. This creates a non-equivalent measure across waves, which violates the assumption of measurement invariance required for valid cross-lagged comparisons. The authors do not test for measurement invariance, do not explain how this missing item was handled in the composite score, and do not discuss the implications for comparability of RWA scores across time points.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The cross-lagged panel model assumes that constructs are measured equivalently across all five time points (measurement invariance). The authors do not test for configural, metric, or scalar invariance. Without establishing measurement invariance, it is impossible to determine whether observed changes over time reflect true change in the latent constructs or changes in how participants interpret and respond to items.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion with potential attrition bias
issues.description: The authors use listwise deletion for missing data. With a longitudinal study spanning five years, attrition is likely substantial, and listwise deletion can introduce serious bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR). The authors do not report attrition rates, do not test whether missingness is random, and do not justify the use of listwise deletion over full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation, which are standard in longitudinal SEM.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The sentence 'We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' appears to be repeated verbatim later in the same paragraph ('Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point'). This suggests careless writing and raises questions about whether the model specification is accurately described.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The authors state they 'adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings' because of the 'large sample size of this dataset', but then report results using p < .01 as the threshold in Figure 1. This is internally inconsistent. Furthermore, with a large sample, the concern should be about inflated Type I error and the need for more stringent thresholds or effect size emphasis, not relaxed thresholds. The stated rationale is backwards.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent reporting of standard errors vs. standard deviations
issues.description: In the Results, the authors report 'B = -.11, SD = .01' and similar statistics. In the context of regression coefficients, 'SD' almost certainly refers to the standard error (SE) of the coefficient, not a standard deviation. This is a systematic mislabeling that could confuse readers and suggests imprecision in statistical reporting.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The reported confidence interval for the RWA predictor is [-.05, -.01], but the point estimate is -.02. This CI is asymmetric around the point estimate in a way that is unusual (lower bound is .03 away, upper bound is .01 away). More importantly, the lower bound of -.05 seems inconsistent with the reported SE of .01 for a 95% CI. This warrants checking for reporting errors.

The chi-square difference test comparing the SDO-RWA cross-lagged paths yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square difference of over 15,000 on 1 degree of freedom is extraordinarily large and almost certainly a reporting error. This value is implausible given the scale of the model and the magnitude of the coefficients involved, and undermines confidence in the accuracy of all reported statistics.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The authors compare a constrained model (SDO→WILL path = RWA→WILL path) to the unconstrained model and find non-significant chi-square difference (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), yet conclude that 'SDO is a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA.' A non-significant model comparison test means the data do not support the claim that the two paths differ statistically. The authors cannot simultaneously accept the null of no difference in the model comparison and then claim SDO is a significantly stronger predictor.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The authors use a traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) without acknowledging its well-documented limitations. The CLPM confounds within-person change with between-person differences. The random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) is now considered the appropriate approach for separating trait-like stability from within-person dynamics. The authors' conclusions about causal influence are therefore potentially invalid, as the cross-lagged paths may reflect between-person differences rather than within-person change.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The abstract and introduction frame the study as examining 'environmentalism' and 'concern for the environment', but the measure used ('willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' / 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment') is a behavioral intention measure, not an attitudinal or concern measure. The two-item scale described ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?') appears to measure concern, not behavioral willingness. There is inconsistency throughout the paper about what is actually being measured.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale... 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: The environmentalism construct is measured with only two items. Two-item scales have well-known psychometric limitations: they cannot be evaluated for internal consistency in the traditional sense (Cronbach's alpha with two items is entirely determined by the inter-item correlation), they cannot be subjected to factor analysis, and they are highly susceptible to item-specific variance. The authors do not justify this choice or acknowledge these limitations.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'.

issues.description: Figure 1 is referenced throughout the Results section as containing the path coefficients and model parameters, but the figure itself is not included in the manuscript. Readers and reviewers cannot evaluate the model results without this figure. This is a critical omission for a paper whose primary contribution is a path model.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL). All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: Table 1 is referenced and its structure described, but the actual data cells appear to be missing or incompletely presented in the manuscript. The table shows only the diagonal (reliability coefficients) and some correlations, but it is unclear whether all values are present as submitted.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: Descriptive statistics (means, SDs, reliabilities, correlations) are only reported for Time 1. For a five-wave longitudinal study, descriptive statistics across all time points are essential for evaluating whether the sample changed over time, whether there are floor/ceiling effects, and whether the constructs show expected patterns of stability and change.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The authors state they 'present standardized parameters' in the Data Analysis section, but then report only unstandardized coefficients (B) in the Results. Standardized coefficients are needed to compare the relative magnitude of SDO vs. RWA effects, which is a central aim of the paper. The authors' comparison of effect sizes using unstandardized coefficients is potentially misleading if the predictors have different variances.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.description: Despite using a cross-lagged panel model (which cannot establish causation), the authors repeatedly make causal claims throughout the Discussion. Phrases like 'causal pathway', 'causal effect', 'SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes', and 'foundational for these attitudes' go beyond what the design supports. Cross-lagged associations are consistent with causal interpretations but do not establish causation.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The model includes only three variables (SDO, RWA, environmentalism). Known confounders such as political orientation, socioeconomic status, age, education, and values (e.g., conservation vs. self-enhancement) are not controlled for. Cross-lagged associations in the absence of relevant covariates may reflect spurious relationships driven by these omitted variables. The authors briefly acknowledge third-variable explanations in the Discussion but do not address this as a limitation of the current model.
issues.quote: Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.

issues.description: The study spans five years across five time points, but the exact timing of each measurement wave is not specified beyond 'five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)'. The intervals between waves are not reported. Unequal or unspecified intervals are problematic for cross-lagged models, as the magnitude of lagged effects depends on the lag length. The stationarity assumption (equal effects across all lags) is particularly questionable if intervals are unequal.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The authors impose a stationary model (all cross-lagged paths constrained to equality across time) without testing whether this assumption holds. They justify this by saying they are 'more interested in the overall and comparative effects', but this does not validate the assumption. If effects change over time (e.g., due to political events, aging of participants, or historical context), the constrained model will produce biased estimates. A test of the stationarity assumption against an unconstrained model should be reported.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The authors state that Mplus syntax 'will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript' but do not mention pre-registration, data availability, or open materials beyond syntax. For a longitudinal study making causal claims, pre-registration would be particularly important. The conditional availability of syntax (only upon acceptance) is also not consistent with open science norms.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The Discussion extensively discusses environmental racism, environmental inequality, and the IPCC's findings about differential climate impacts on the poor. While potentially relevant background, this material is not connected to any hypothesis tested in the study, no data are presented on these topics, and the discussion reads as tangential. This section appears to be padding that does not follow from the empirical findings.
issues.quote: Bryant [35] noted that environmental racism occurs when people of colour are disproportionately exposed to environmental hazards... Pellow [36] takes this idea a step further in defining environmental inequality as more strongly tied to social hierarchy...

issues.description: The abstract states 'RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor' and the conclusion states the desire to 'submit to authority and tradition' leads to lower environmentalism. However, the Results show that the model comparison test for SDO vs. RWA paths was non-significant (p = .126), meaning the data do not statistically support the claim that SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA. The framing of RWA as definitively 'weaker' is not supported by the formal statistical test.
issues.quote: RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor.

issues.description: The autoregressive (stability) paths are described qualitatively ('relatively stable over time') but no numerical values are reported in the text. For a paper whose first prediction is about stability of these constructs, the actual stability coefficients should be reported with confidence intervals.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.description: Even if the sample were a genuine national probability sample of New Zealand adults, the authors' generalizability claims extend beyond New Zealand to broader theoretical conclusions about SDO, RWA, and environmentalism globally. New Zealand has a specific political context (noted by Duckitt [3] as having a highly polarized political system) that may not generalize to other countries. The authors acknowledge this only briefly.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The manuscript contains multiple typographical errors including 'sarcity' (should be 'scarcity'), 'situatoinal' (should be 'situational'), 'nonexistant' (should be 'nonexistent'), 'stonger' (should be 'stronger'), 'analagous' (should be 'analogous'), and 'effect' used where 'affect' is correct ('effect people's livelihoods'). These errors suggest insufficient proofreading.
issues.quote: resource sarcity and economic recession increases intergroup conflict... These situatoinal factors could also reasonably motivate self-serving behaviours... effect people's livelihoods

issues.description: Throughout the Results section, chi-square statistics are formatted as '2(1)' rather than 'χ²(1)', suggesting a formatting/encoding error where the Greek letter chi and superscript 2 were lost. This makes the statistics difficult to read and suggests the manuscript was not carefully proofread in its final format.

The authors use six items from the SDO6 scale. However, the SDO7 scale (Ho et al., 2015) distinguishes between SDO-Dominance and SDO-Egalitarianism subscales, which have been shown to have differential relationships with environmentalism (as noted in the authors' own reference [24]). Using the older SDO6 without acknowledging this limitation or the potential differential effects of the two dimensions is a missed opportunity and limits the theoretical contribution.
issues.quote: Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto's [1] SDO6 scale.

issues.description: The authors constrain residual variances for the same item to be equal across time points. This is a strong assumption that implies homoscedasticity of measurement error across all five waves. This assumption is not tested and may not hold, particularly given the five-year span and the missing item at Time 2 for RWA. Violation of this assumption would bias the model estimates.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The finding that RWA predicts SDO but not vice versa is interpreted as meaning 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This interpretation is speculative and not supported by the data. The asymmetric cross-lagged relationship could reflect many things, including differential measurement reliability, range restriction, or the specific political context of the 2009-2013 period in New Zealand. The authors present this as a substantive conclusion without adequate justification.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander's are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.subcategory: reference to unpublished/in-press work as if established
issues.description: The paper cites Stanley and Wilson [22] as a meta-analysis that establishes key findings used to motivate the study's hypotheses. Reference [22] appears to be in press at time of submission (doi provided but no volume/page numbers). Relying heavily on an in-press paper by the same authors to justify predictions creates a circularity concern and means reviewers cannot fully evaluate the evidentiary basis for the hypotheses.
issues.quote: Stanley SK, Wilson MS. Meta-analysing the association between social dominance orientation, authoritarianism, and attitudes on the environment and climate change. J Env Psych. 2019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2018.12.002

issues.description: The study spans 2009-2013, a period that included significant global events relevant to both environmental attitudes (Copenhagen climate summit failure in 2009, various IPCC reports) and economic conditions (global financial crisis aftermath). These historical events could systematically influence all three variables and their relationships over time. The authors do not discuss how historical context might affect their findings or the stationarity assumption.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: Participants were approximately 19 years old at Time 1 and approximately 24 at Time 5. This means the study conflates longitudinal change with developmental/maturational change. Young adults in their early-to-mid twenties undergo significant identity development, political socialization, and life transitions (e.g., entering the workforce, completing education). Any observed changes in SDO, RWA, or environmentalism could reflect developmental processes rather than the reciprocal causal influences the authors claim.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31)
